name: Steep Ravine Cabins & Environmental Camp
description: Perched dramatically on rocky coastal cliffs directly above the crashing Pacific surf. Features iconic rustic redwood cabins with wood-burning stoves, panoramic ocean sunsets, and secret tide pools below.
tip: Reservations drop 6 months in advance at 8:00 AM PST and sell out in seconds. Mid-week dates and winter wave watching offer your best chance.

name: Pantoll Campground
description: Nestled in a peaceful Douglas fir and redwood glade right at the intersection of the legendary Dipsea, Matt Davis, and Steep Ravine trails. Epic trailhead access.
tip: Arrive before 9:00 AM on Friday morning to secure a site for the weekend. Bring exact cash or pay at the ranger station self-pay kiosk.

name: Bootjack Campground
description: Set among mossy oak woodlands and whispering redwoods along Bootjack Creek. Direct connection to the Mountain Theater and Muir Woods trails.
tip: Less crowded than Pantoll, yet only 1 mile away. Perfect backup when Pantoll fills up early.

name: Kirby Cove Campground
description: Tucked inside a sheltered eucalyptus grove with breathtaking million-dollar views of the Golden Gate Bridge and the San Francisco skyline right from the beach.
tip: Campers get a combination code for the gated access road. It is a steep 1-mile descent down to the cove, so pack compact gear.
hike_in_distance: Drive-in with gate code / 1.0 mi walk-in

name: Bicentennial Campground
description: The most urban yet wild coastal campsite in America. Just 100 yards from the road above Horseshoe Cove with views across the bay towards San Francisco.
tip: No wood or charcoal fires permitted; only gas camp stoves allowed. Strong coastal fog winds roll in by 4 PM, so stake your tent securely.

name: Hawkcamp Campground
description: High on an exposed windswept ridge overlooking Rodeo Valley and Gerbode Valley. Outstanding stargazing and raptor watching during autumn hawk migrations.
tip: No water available; you MUST pack in all your drinking and cooking water. 3-mile uphill hike from Tennessee Valley trailhead.

name: Haypress Campground
description: Situated in an idyllic meadow framed by eucalyptus and coastal willows in Tennessee Valley, just a flat 0.75-mile walk from the trailhead parking.
tip: Perfect first-time backpacking trip for kids and beginners. No potable water on site, carry water from the trailhead water station.

name: Samuel P. Taylor State Park (Camp Taylor)
sites_count: 60 sites, plus rustic cabins & group camp
description: Deep in the tranquil heart of San Geronimo Valley amidst towering coastal redwoods along Lagunitas Creek. Paved Cross Marin bike path runs right by camp.
tip: Cabin sites provide heated bunk beds without electricity. In winter, watch Coho salmon spawn in the creek right behind camp!

name: Back Ranch Meadows Campground
description: Sheltered in a sunny oak and bay laurel woodland on the shores of San Pablo Bay. Renowned for its warm microclimate, mountain biking loops, and historic Chinese shrimp village.
tip: Cart wheelbarrows are provided in the parking lot to haul gear to your walk-in campsite (50-200 yards). Far less foggy than coastal Marin.

name: Coast Camp
description: Nestled in a gentle coastal valley just 200 meters from wild, windswept Santa Maria Beach. Fall asleep to the rhythmic roar of Pacific breakers.
tip: Bike-in camping is permitted via Coast Trail from Laguna Trailhead (2.7 miles, gentle gravel fire road). Bring driftwood permits for beach campfires.

name: Wildcat Camp
description: Located in an open meadow plateau above Wildcat Beach. The ultimate gateway to Alamere Falls, the famous coastal tidefall waterfall cascading directly onto the sand.
tip: Alamere Falls is an easy 1.1-mile stroll south along the beach at low tide. Check tide charts carefully before setting out.

name: Sky Camp
description: Perched high on the western shoulder of Mount Wittenberg. Sweeping vistas across Drakes Bay, the Pacific Ocean, and the Point Reyes peninsula.
tip: Only 1.4 miles uphill from Sky Trailhead. Pack warm windbreakers as mountain fog moves in fast during twilight.

name: Glen Camp
description: Deep in a secluded, quiet wooded valley protected from chilly ocean winds by high surrounding ridges. Shaded by Douglas fir, ferns, and bay trees.
tip: The most wind-protected camp in Point Reyes. No beach access directly from camp, but peaceful solitude is unmatched.

name: Angel Island State Park Campgrounds
description: An unforgettable island camping experience in the middle of San Francisco Bay. Breathtaking night views of the lit-up downtown skyline, Golden Gate, and Bay Bridge.
tip: Take the Tiburon or SF ferry. Sites 4 and 5 offer the most spectacular direct views of the Golden Gate Bridge. Wood fires strictly prohibited.
hike_in_distance: 1.5 to 2.5 mi hike-in from Ayala Cove Ferry Dock

name: Anthony Chabot Family Campground
description: Set on a high ridge overlooking peaceful Lake Chabot surrounded by fragrant eucalyptus and pine. Miles of hiking trails, fishing, and boating just downhill.
tip: Walk-in sites #65-#74 nestled along Two Rocks trail offer the most shade and secluded nature feel.

name: Del Valle Family Campground
description: A huge, sun-drenched lakeside park tucked into the rolling golden hills of Livermore. Famous for swimming beaches, boat rentals, and the eastern gateway to the Ohlone Wilderness Trail.
tip: Sites in the Cedar loop have the best tree cover for hot summer afternoons. Bring kayaks or paddleboards!

name: Mount Diablo - Juniper Campground
description: Perched high on the mountain at 3,000 feet elevation with staggering sunset views sweeping across the entire Bay Area, Golden Gate, and the Farallon Islands.
tip: Sites 11-17 hug the western rim with unobstructed sunset vistas over the clouds. Nights can be breezy; pack warm layers.

name: Mount Diablo - Live Oak Campground
description: Tucked inside the intriguing sandstone formations of Rock City among native valley oaks. Ideal base for bouldering and exploring Wind Caves.
tip: Kids love scrambling around Rock City and Sentinel Rock right next to camp. More wind-sheltered than Juniper.

name: Sunol Wilderness Backpack Camp
description: Set in a rugged, remote oak canyon near the rushing waters of Alameda Creek. A highlight stop along the 28-mile Ohlone Wilderness Trail.
tip: Requires an Ohlone Wilderness Trail Permit ($4/yr). Spring wildflowers and green hills here rival Scotland.
hike_in_distance: 3.2 mi hike-in from Sunol Visitor Center

name: Rose Peak / Maggie's Half Acre Trail Camp
description: Resting just below the summit of Rose Peak (3,817 ft)—only 32 feet lower than Mount Diablo! True wilderness solitude in the deep East Bay backcountry.
tip: Serious 10-mile, 3,500 ft climb from Del Valle or Sunol. Bring sturdy water filter and trekking poles.

name: Stewartville Backpack Camp
description: Surrounded by historic 19th-century coal and silica sand mining territory and the historic Rose Hill Cemetery under wide, star-studded skies.
tip: You must pack in all drinking water. Pair with an underground Hazel-Atlas silica sand mine tour during the day.

name: Francis Beach Campground
description: Set right on coastal bluffs directly overlooking Half Moon Bay's sweeping sandy beach. Watch whales migrate while relaxing by your campfire.
tip: Campground sits directly on the paved Coastal Trail; bring bikes to cruise north into Princeton Harbor or south along the bluffs.

name: Rob Hill Campground
description: The only overnight campground in the city of San Francisco! Perched in a historic cypress grove above Baker Beach with views through the trees to the Pacific.
tip: Open April 1 through October 31. Great for scout troops, family reunions, and tech team offsites.

name: Ben Ries Campground
description: A secluded redwood sanctuary tucked away in a quiet coastal canyon near Pescadero. Lush sword ferns, babbling Little Butano Creek, and cool marine air.
tip: Walk-in sites #22-#39 feel like deep backcountry but are only 50-100 yards from parking. Stop in Pescadero for famous artichoke bread!

name: Portola Redwoods Campground
description: Hidden in an extraordinarily quiet canyon where Peter's Creek and Pescadero Creek merge. Massive 300-foot ancient redwoods and Tip Toe Falls.
tip: Zero cell service in the canyon—a true peaceful escape. Access is via a winding narrow mountain road; trailers over 21ft prohibited.

name: Memorial County Park Campground
description: San Mateo County's crown-jewel redwood park since 1924. Features a newly renovated campground along Pescadero Creek, camp store, and campfire amphitheater.
tip: Recently underwent a multi-million-dollar renovation with ADA-accessible sites, modern restrooms, and upgraded water systems.

name: Black Mountain Backpack Camp
description: Tucked into a quiet oak and bay grove just 0.5 miles below the 2,800-foot summit of Black Mountain. Stunning nighttime vistas across Silicon Valley and Stanford.
tip: A quick 1.5-mile hike from Page Mill Road parking makes this the easiest introductory backpacking camp on the Peninsula.

name: Castle Rock Trail Camp
description: Surrounded by bizarre tafoni sandstone caves, sculpted boulders, and redwood forests at 3,000 feet along the crest of the Santa Cruz Mountains.
tip: A scenic 2.6-mile hike from the modern Robert C. Kirkwood entrance. Key stop on the Skyline-to-the-Sea trail.

name: Sanborn County Park Campground
description: Nestled in dense second-growth redwoods on the coastal slope of Saratoga Gap. Lush green year-round with wandering banana slugs and flowing creeks.
tip: Sites #1-#15 are a short 100-yard walk from parking. Combine with the hike up to Saratoga Gap and Castle Rock.

name: Mount Madonna County Park (Tan Oak & Valley View)
description: High on the southern Santa Cruz Mountains crest above Gilroy and Watsonville. Majestic redwood groves, Henry Miller historic ruins, and rare white fallow deer pens.
tip: Rent one of the canvas yurts with bunk beds, wrap-around redwood decks, and dome skylights for an effortless glamping trip!

name: Joseph D. Grant County Park (Halls Valley)
description: Set in a broad, golden valley below Mount Hamilton and Lick Observatory. Sprawling oak grasslands, Bass Lake fishing, and roaming herds of tule elk.
tip: Outstanding dark night skies ideal for setting up a personal telescope. Scenic 20-minute drive up to Lick Observatory on the peak.

name: Uvas Canyon County Park Campground
description: Tucked inside a steep, lush canyon on the eastern slopes of the Santa Cruz Mountains. Famous for Swanson Creek's series of six picturesque cascades and waterfalls.
tip: Best in late winter and spring when the waterfalls are roaring. Even day visitors need advance parking reservations, so camping guarantees access.

name: Little Basin Cabins & Campground
description: A beautiful 530-acre preserve originally built as an employee retreat by Hewlett-Packard, now part of Big Basin. Cozy rustic cabins nestled beneath towering coastal redwoods.
tip: One of the quickest ways to stay in the Big Basin redwood canopy as the park recovers and reopens from the CZU fire.

name: Big Basin Redwoods - Huckleberry & Blooms Creek
description: California's very first state park, founded in 1902. Witness the awe-inspiring regeneration of centuries-old ancient giant redwoods flourishing with vibrant green sprouts.
tip: Advance day-use and camping reservations required through the park's reopening system. Check latest trail opening maps at headquarters.

name: Henry Cowell Redwoods Campground
description: Nestled in a fragrant pine and oak sand-hill ridge just above the breathtaking ancient Old Growth Redwood Grove along the San Lorenzo River in Felton.
tip: Walk right from camp onto the River Trail to see giant redwoods and hear the historic Roaring Camp steam train whistle echoing through the canyon.

name: New Brighton State Beach Campground
description: Perched on pine-studded coastal bluffs with panoramic vistas over the gentle, warmer waters of Monterey Bay. Private footpath leads directly onto wide sandy Capitola beach.
tip: Sites #74-#82 are front-row bluff sites with direct Pacific views. Stroll along the sand right into Capitola Village for fish tacos and ice cream.

name: Seacliff State Beach
description: Legendary beach campsite famous for the historic concrete freighter 'SS Palo Alto'. Park your rig literally steps from the surf line on Monterey Bay.
tip: Self-contained RV and trailer camping only (no ground tents). Incredible morning ocean walks and sea otter spotting.

name: Manresa Uplands Campground
description: A peaceful tent-only coastal sanctuary situated on rolling sandstone bluffs overlooking miles of untouched Monterey Bay beaches. No RVs allowed.
tip: Campers carry gear ~100-300 yards from parking (bring collapsible wagons). Enjoy magnificent sunset bonfires on the sand.

name: Sunset State Beach Campground
description: Nestled behind towering coastal sand dunes and fragrant Monterey pine forests. Wide-open sunsets, remote beachcombing, and soothing surf sounds.
tip: The Dunes camp loop is closest to the wooden staircase down to the beach. Much quieter than northern Santa Cruz county beaches.

name: Costanoa Coastal Lodge & KOA
sites_count: Tent sites, luxury canvas tent cabins & lodge
description: An eco-adventure coastal resort offering everything from pitcher-pump tent sites to deluxe safari tent bungalows with heated mattress pads and spa treatments.
tip: Adjacent to Franklin Point and Ano Nuevo State Reserve (elephant seals). Perfect mix of rugged nature and boutique luxury.

name: Santa Cruz Redwoods RV Resort
description: Nestled directly on the banks of the San Lorenzo River beneath a soaring canopy of coastal redwoods. Clean, quiet, and family-friendly.
tip: Riverfront sites have private decks overlooking the swimming holes. 10 minutes to downtown Santa Cruz and the Boardwalk.

name: Veterans Memorial Park Campground
description: Tucked among Monterey pines high above the historic bay, just 1.5 miles from Cannery Row and the Monterey Bay Aquarium.
tip: First-come, first-served year-round. Arrive by 11:00 AM on summer weekends for the best pine-shaded sites.

name: Pinnacles National Park Campground
description: Surrounded by ancient volcanic rock spires, talus caves, and soaring California Condors. Exceptional dark-sky stargazing and rugged hiking.
tip: Campground has its own seasonal swimming pool and camp store. Bring headlamps for exploring Bear Gulch and Balconies Caves!

name: Henry W. Coe - Manzanita Point
description: Spaced generously across a panoramic ridge dotted with manzanita, blue oaks, and Bass Pond. Absolute peace and dark skies.
tip: A gentle 2.5-mile hike along Springs Trail from Coe Headquarters. Unmatched tranquility with sprawling Diablo range views.

name: San Luis Reservoir (Basalt Campground)
description: Set on a sheltered plateau near the base of San Luis Dam along historic Pacheco Pass. Renowned for sailing, windsurfing, and trophy striped bass fishing.
tip: Windsurfers flock to O'Neill Forebay nearby. Watch for herds of tule elk roaming the reservoir shorelines in early morning.

name: Saddle Mountain Ranch & Cabins
description: Perched above sunny Carmel Valley on 89 secluded wooded acres. Heated pool, hiking trails through eucalyptus, and 10 minutes to Carmel beach.
tip: Warmer and sunnier than the coastal beaches. Ideal base for exploring Point Lobos State Reserve.

name: Laguna Seca Recreation Area Campground
description: Set in the rolling oak savannah foothills between Monterey and Salinas. Miles of mountain biking and hiking trails in the Fort Ord National Monument adjacent.
tip: Direct trail gate connects to the 86 miles of trails in Fort Ord National Monument. Avoid race weekends unless you love motorsport!
